subsubtopic: CALL FOR DISBANDMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the establishment of the Macdonald Royal Commission on the economy was a shrug of the shoulders in the direction of the more than 1.5 million Canadians out of work, and a slap in the face to the already excessively tax-burdened workers who will have to pay the estimated $10 million to $15 million cost of the Commission. If the Government is allowed to continue its destructive economic policies, in three years the number of unemployed will have doubled and those Canadians actually able to pay their spiralling taxes will have become an endangered species. I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis):
That the Government immediately disband this cosmetic and costly Commission and, to demonstrate its trust in Canadians, call a general election which would permit the people of Canada to choose the right solution to our economic ills.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Finance. The Minister of Finance agreed with this yesterday. He said nothing about how a new interest rate policy would be followed in order to avoid this past disaster. Would the Minister say now what that new policy will be, so that Canadians can judge better for themselves whether these disasters of 20 per cent-plus interest rates will be repeated in the future?

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT BENEFITS BE EXTENDED
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. On Monday the Minister of Finance refused to extend unemployment insurance benefits to unemployed Canadians whose benefits had expired but who are still unable to get jobs. Since then I have learned of a case in British Columbia involving a particular worker who worked for 13 years but who has lost his job and is now losing his home, and whose unemployment insurance benefits are about to run out. This man, like thousands of other workers, first wants a job. If he cannot get that, then he
Oral Questions
would like the right to unemployment insurance and not be forced onto welfare.
Will the Prime Minister take the opportunity, before we recess for Christmas, to correct the Minister of Finance and assure the people of Canada that the Government wiil extend U.I. benefits so that workers will have the right to them, at least, and will not be forced to go onto welfare?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT BENEFITS BE EXTENDED
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I cannot add anything to what the Minister said yesterday. We have attempted to deal with the so-called exhaustees by trying to find work for them so that they could qualify for regular jobs or, failing that, re-enter the unemployment insurance rolls. However, insofar as providing jobs for every unemployed worker in Canada is concerned, whether or not he or she has been on unemployment insurance, I am afraid that the Minister of Finance conceded that we did not have that kind of money. So-

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT BENEFITS BE EXTENDED
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I wish the Prime Minister would listen with care to the question. The question was not about jobs, as such. The question, in this instance, was about unemployment insurance benefits.

I would therefore like to come back to the Prime Minister and say that, before Christmas, thousands of working families will be forced, for the first time in their lives, to go onto welfare because they are not entitled, according to the law as it now exists, to unemployment insurance benefits. Considering the fact that the federal Government already picks up the major share of welfare costs, and considering the fact that workers would rather have unemployment insurance, why does the Government not do the appropriate thing, which makes sense and is socially desirable, and extend the unemployment insurance scheme for all the workers who, unfortunately, will need financial assistance?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, if the Hon. Member refers with care to the answer I gave, I think he will find that I dealt with that. It is a question of making money available to do what the Hon. Member suggests, and we do not have that money available.

subsubtopic: QUEBECAIR 2-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport and concerns Quebecair. When the Minister of Transport announced his solution for Quebecair, the company's employees made it clear that they intended to meet with the Minister. I should like to know whether they still intend to do so, and also whether the Quebec spokesman, Mr. Leblond, has been in touch with the Minister of Transport. What is the present status of the Quebecair question?

subsubtopic: QUEBECAIR 2-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Quebec Minister of Transport, Mr. Clair, has stated publicly that he was satisfied with my explanations regarding a number of areas. However, there is still one question on which we have not been able to agree, and that is whether negotiations should focus on creating a new company or on restructuring the existing one. My thoughts on the issue are quite clear. I think that if we try to restructure the previous company, with all the financial obligations with which it is burdened, including its debt to the Government of Quebec, to Mr. Webster, to Mr. Hamel, to Mr. Provost, and so on, the company will never get off the ground. On the other hand, I can hardly refuse to give Mr. Clair an opportunity to defend the opposite view. It will not be easy for him but I can hardly prevent him from doing so. So that is where we are now, and we are going to try to clear up our differences this afternoon. As far as the status of Quebecair employees is concerned, in the note I sent Mr. Clair a few days ago, I undertook on behalf of the Government to give them some form of protection. Of
course, I was not very specific, and for good reason, since I must be careful to avoid making any commitments we cannot honour in other cases as well. So that is where we are now with the employees. Mr. Leblond was appointed by the Quebec Government as the intermediary in this question, and we shall have our own negotiator as well on this task force which is to be created very shortly.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subsubtopic: EFFECT OF INTEREST RATE POLICY ON HOME OWNERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Finance. For the better part of a year the Government has been making interest rate policies based on what the Governor of the Bank of Canada now admits was an unreliable guide. As a result, thousands of Canadians lost their homes, not through any fault of their own but because of the Government's mistaken high interest rate policy. What explanation does the Minister have for these thousands of Canadians who lost their homes because of the Government's misguided interest rate policy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of State (Finance)):
subsubtopic: EFFECT OF INTEREST RATE POLICY ON HOME OWNERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I do not believe that the policy of the Governor of the Bank is any different this year than it was last year, or during the year the Leader of the Opposition was Prime Minister of the country. The Hon. Member asking the question has not really characterized the policy of the Governor of the Bank and the posture of the Government of Canada in so far as interest rates and financial policy are concerned. In his statement the Governor of the Bank said that for a number of months the Bank has not used Ml exclusively as the only criterion in applying the policy against inflation and the difficulties that inflation has visited on our economy, including high interest rates and the difficulties that they bring to many people in Canada, not only to home owners but to small-businessmen. The Governor indicated that the M1 characterization was only one of the criteria at which the bank was looking.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO HOME OWNERS

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I agree with the Minister that the high interest rate policy affected not only home owners but farmers, owners of small businesses, and many other Canadians. It was wrong. Not only did it cause thousands of Canadians to lose their homes, but many hundreds of thousands of others are today carrying interest rates at 20, 21 and 22 per cent because of a policy the Governor of the Bank of Canada said was wrong for more than a year. What does the Minister intend to do to
December 1, 1982

compensate those persons who are carrying much higher interest rates and mortgages rates than they should be because of the Government's mistaken policy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of State (Finance)):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I indicated in a previous answer that, since the June budget, interest rates have fallen by approximately 6 per cent. This means that a person with a mortgage of around $50,000, with the interest rates being reduced by 6 per cent, is paying $200 a month less in carrying charges. There has been a remarkable improvement in so far as interest rates are concerned.
It would be trite for me to remind the Hon. Member that the Government, in response to the plight of people during the period of time when interest rates were high, announced a number of programs to assist not only home owners but small businessmen. In the field of home owners renewing their mortgages, there was the Canada Mortgage Renewal Plan, a plan to protect those people who had to pay more than 30 per cent of their income under their newly renewed mortgage contracts. That was a sensible and sensitive response. It was sensitive to people facing that difficulty. It was sensible in that it did not encourage the expenditure of billions of dollars which some people would have had us expend at that time.

subsubtopic: CONDITIONS FOR OBTAINING SUBSIDY FOR DAVIE SHIPBUILDING OF LAUZON, P.Q.
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. Last Sunday, workers at Davie Shipbuilding in Lauzon brought out a majority vote against the 6 and 5 policy. Since the Minister knows perfectly well that this company is awaiting the Government's decision regarding a subsidy of $30 million for the construction of a ferry, could the Minister inform the House whether it is true, that if the union failed to support the Government's 6 and 5 policy, it would not only be in danger of losing but would, in fact, have lost, the $30 million subsidy altogether?

subsubtopic: CONDITIONS FOR OBTAINING SUBSIDY FOR DAVIE SHIPBUILDING OF LAUZON, P.Q.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I shall be happy to answer this question, because it is the first time Hon. Members have acknowledged that my Department is the client in this case. CN Marine has, in fact, decided to invest $100 million in the purchase of this ship. However, the price quoted was in excess of our ability to pay, and we therefore required an additional grant of $30 million from the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. For three months, the Government said that it could not be done because an exceptional contribution by the Government of Canada is necessary to make construction at all possible,
Oral Questions
unless Davie Shipbuilding employees are themselves prepared to make a sacrifice, and we have been repeating this to all and sundry for three months. Well, we are now in a position where we are about to say: This is the deadline, and if you cannot reach a decision before that deadline, we shall have to withdraw our order.

I had understood that the Government's policy vis-a-vis the private sector was one in which the private sector was asked to co-operate with this program, and 1 did not think it was compulsory. Now, if 1 understand the Minister correctly, this policy which was voluntary for the private sector would now be compulsory, according to the Minister's reasoning, namely, that either they agree to observe the 6 and 5 ceiling and they get a contract with a subsidy of $30 million, or they do not, and then 1,000 employees lose out on this construction job. Is that more or less what was meant by the Minister?

I think we all have to realize that this is a case where the Government is using public funds in an effort to remedy a particular situation, namely, to prevent these employees from being laid off. Since the Government is making a special effort to accommodate the interests of these employees, it feels it also has a case for asking or demanding, if my hon. friend prefers, that these employees make a special effort as well. The whole point of the policy is to keep inflation at 6 per cent, and in doing so, they too are helping to achieve this goal. Therefore, 1 do not have the impression, and I do not think Canadians have the impression, that we are taking a particularly hard line with these employees. We are proposing an arrangement that will benefit both sides, and in any case, they will have an opportunity to make up their own minds on the matter.

subsubtopic: CANOLA FREIGHT RATE INCREASES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. I am given to understand that the canola crushers and growers have been notified that the freight rates for canola products are going to be increased by 41 per cent to 42 per cent, both on the CPR and CNR lines. How does the Minister justify this increase to the western farmers in light of the five and six guidelines that the Government has laid down?

subsubtopic: CANOLA FREIGHT RATE INCREASES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, it is quite simple. The Railway Act, Section 276, states that the cost of transportation must exceed the variable costs. In other words, rates cannot ever come under the variable costs. If the CTC had not passed the order that they have passed to increase the minimum compensation rate by 42 per cent, they would have been in violation of the law. The law being the paramount authority in these matters, I think it should prevail.

Madam Speaker, the Minister of Finance yesterday said that five and six was the law of the land. Is it the law of the land, or is it not? In addition, I would like to know whether this will affect imports from the United States coming into eastern Canada, putting the canola growers in western Canada to an unfair advantage in terms of competition? And does the Minister expect that these types of guidelines, 40 per cent and 50 per cent increases, will roll over into the Gilson Report, and other products shipped in western Canada?

December 1, 1982
Oral Questions

Madam Speaker, 1 think the rate is a West to East rate only. I could not swear to that. I am not knowledgeable on that, so I will check, but again I think it applies only to transportation from the West to the East.
The effect that this will have on Gilson is a rather complicated matter. The present rate for transportation of rape-seed or canola oil and meal to the East is the minimum compensatory rate. Gilson recommended that from the West to Thunder Bay it should be the statutory rate in due course. But he did not indicate what it should be from Thunder Bay on to the East. The logic of the system would indicate that it should be commercial rates at that point. It so happens that if you put the statutory rate to Thunder Bay and the commercial rate from Thunder Bay on East, you have a higher rate than the rate you have now, which is the minimum compensatory rate all the way. There is an obvious problem with that, and we will try to solve it in due course, when we make our announcement on the implementation of the Western Rail Transportation Initiative.

subsubtopic: PURPOSE OF MEASURE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to put a question to the Prime Minister with regard to Bill S-3I which regulates provincial involvement in transportation. The Province of Quebec has indicated that it is opposed to the legislation, the Province of Alberta has indicated that it is also opposed to the legislation, and Pierre Lortie has also indicated that he is opposed to the legislation. Mr. Lortie, of course, is an adviser to the Government on other matters.
It appears that only Canadian Pacific is vitally concerned about the passage of this legislation. Why is Canadian Pacific's vested interest more important than the expressed interests of the Provinces most affected and the interest of the President of the Montreal Stock Exchange?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: PURPOSE OF MEASURE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the main purpose of the legislation is to discourage Provinces from exercising extraterritorial jurisdiction. The Provinces, under the Constitution, cannot make laws or adopt policies having to do with interprovincial or international transportation. They would become enabled to do so if they were able to acquire control of, and to issue policy directives to, an interprovincial or international corporation. They would be going around the Constitution in a way that the federal Government finds it undesirable to allow.

Madam Speaker, I will put a supplementary question to the Prime Minister. He knows full well that the federal Government has the power to
regulate, at any time, in the national interest. Given that, if there appeared to be a problem developing, the federal Government could establish such regulations as to make sure that the problem did not mature, why would the Government think it more appropriate that foreign investors from any part of the world should be able to own the interprovincial trucking and transportation industry in Canada, if they so desire, and not feel it appropriate that the duly elected representatives of the Provinces, who are responsible to the Canadian public, ought to be able to make decisions, similarly, to have investment in Canada's future?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is because, presumably, the foreign interest or, for that matter, the private sector interest in operating a railway or exercising a degree of control over an interprovincial or international industry, is to make money, to make profits. The purpose of the federal Government is to issue policies which ensure that that objective does not enter into conflict with the national good of the Canadian people, in other words, that the service be provided. If the control is exercised by a provincial Government, I presume the Member would agree that the first purpose of the provincial Government is not to make money or to make profits for its shareholders, but to exercise political directions. If this is the objective of the provincial Governments, to exercise political directions on interprovincial railways, we feel this is regrettable.
The Hon. Member is, of course, correct. The federal Government could step in and start a fight with the Provinces and sort of say, "You should not be running the railway which you control in this way because, for instance, you are asking to move the head office of the CPR from Montreal to some other city in Canada", and we would get into an interprovincial conflict in an area-
Oh, oh!

Madam Speaker, I understand that the Hon. Member does not want to hear my answers but I want to assure him that it is an important subject of ensuring that there is no extraterritorial application by the stronger Provinces against the weak ones. This would happen if they can control an interprovincial transportation company.

subsubtopic: TAX RETURNS OF MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
1.	With reference to the answer to Question No. 2,564 which stated in part that "no statistics are available" in regard to the number of income tax returns by Members of Parliament that were in any way re-examined or re-assessed by the Department of National Revenue, are the tax returns of all Members of Parliament and Senators in the hands of one specific individual in the Department of National Revenue and, if so, for what reason is it impossible for the government to have statistics available on the number of such returns that have been dealt with over and above the original assessment?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):
subsubtopic: TAX RETURNS OF MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
1.
The tax returns of Members of Parliament, like those of any other taxpayer, are filed in various District Offices and Taxation Centres according to the place of residence of the taxpayer and therefore are not in the hands of one specific individual. However, all returns of Members of Parliament filed in the Ottawa District Office are in the custody of a single individual as a matter of local practice. Statistics on the total numbers of reassessments are maintained and the number of reassessments by board occupational groups, but not for small groups such as Members of Parliament.
2. Access to the tax files of Members of Parliament is not made by government order. Access is accorded as required for the same reasons as apply to all files of taxpayers and is restricted to officials as authorized under Section 241 of the Income Tax Act.

speechtext:

subsubtopic: TRANSPORTATION AND TRAVELLING EXPENSES
speechtext: With reference to the Budget of November 12, 1981, which announced that free airline transportation provided by employers would be considered taxable as income, will this provision apply to Cabinet Ministers using such transportation to go to and from their constituencies or elsewhere, when not on Government business and when exceeding the quota of trips permitted for Members of Parliament to and from their constituencies, and (a) if so, what will be the effective date (b) if not, for what reason?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pierre Bussieres (Minister of National Revenue):
subsubtopic: TRANSPORTATION AND TRAVELLING EXPENSES
speechtext: Subparagraph 6(l)(b)(i)(A) of the Income Tax Act excludes from income from office or employment amounts received in the year as an allowance for personal or living expenses or as an allowance for any other purpose that is expressly fixed in an Act of the Parliament of Canada. Subsection 43(1) of the Senate and House of Commons Act refers to transportation and travelling expenses as each House may by order prescribe. Therefore, the value of any transportation or reimbursement of transportation and travelling expenses specifically prescribed and covered in the latter mentioned Act is not taxable. In addition the value of any transportation or reimbursement of such specific expenses to Members of the Senate and House of Commons incurred while on government business is not taxable. When the transportation is for personal as opposed to business use, a taxable benefit arises.

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: FAMILY ALLOWANCES ACT, 1973 MEASURE TO LIMIT INDEXATION
speechtext:
that Bill C-132, an Act to amend the Family Allowances Act, 1973, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.
She said: Madam Speaker, I am pleased to introduce Bill C-132. This Bill is one of a series of initiatives which were announced in the budget of June, 1982. The changes in the Family Allowances Program which are outlined in this Bill,

December 1, 1982
Family Allowances Act, 1973
together with similar changes to the Old Age Security Act, the Income Tax Act and a number of other related Acts, comprise what has now become known as the Government's "six and five" program. The changes to these Acts were offered only after the most careful consideration on the part of the Government, but with the full realization that the way to defeat inflation for Canadian families and the way to economic recovery requires some degree of sacrifice by all Canadians. Family Allowance recipients-in other words, mothers-are among those many Canadians being asked to make this sacrifice. 1 repeat the expression I used for the Bill reducing the indexation for seniors who do not need the supplement- that they are being asked to make a sacrifice with others.
Although the modifications in child-related benefits contained in this Bill are relatively modest, we are confident that the example being set by Family Allowance recipients, by mothers across the country-which means by lots of families-and by pensioners, civil servants, Members of Parliament and taxpayers, as part of a national will to fight inflation, will be followed by all Canadians.
What does this Bill do? 1 will say exactly what it does in the hope that Opposition colleagues who want to speak on the Bill will limit their speeches, as provided for by the rules of the Fiouse, to the Bill in question and not carry on with misinformation in the way that took place during the discussion on the Bill concerning old age pensions.
Specifically, this Bill proposes to limit, only for those who can afford it, the indexation of Family Allowances to a 6 per cent cost-of-living adjustment in 1983 and a 5 per cent adjustment the year after. Right now, the Family Allowance payment is $26.91 per month per child. When families receive their cheques on approximately January 20, the amount payable for each child will be $28.52. This will rise to $29.95 the year after.
Flon. Members will recall that Alberta and Quebec have opted on their own to vary the federal rate. Therefore, the amount per child will differ somewhat in those Provinces.
As a consequence of this Bill, only one-third of Canadian mothers receiving Family Allowances will get a smaller increase than anticipated for their child benefits in the coming two years. 1 want to emphasize the fact that this Bill permits an increase in all Family Allowances for the next year, indexation has not been eliminated completely; the principles of universality and indexation are maintained. Furthermore, we have acted to ensure that all families in the low income range and younger families in the middle income range will not be adversely affected by this two-year measure. The previous Minister of Finance stated this clearly in his June budget, and 1 also explained in an insert which was mailed with the Family Allowance cheques at a later date that the Child Tax Credit in 1982, which is to be received early next year, will be fully indexed to the cost of living.
In addition, all recipients of the Child Tax Credit, which are two-thirds of Canadian mothers, will receive a one-time special
increase of $50 which will be added to the credit in order to compensate for the capping of indexation of their Family Allowances. This means that the two-thirds of all mothers who receive the full Child Tax Credit will receive $343 in the coming months instead of the indexed $293 that they would have normally received. They received far less last year. While they would have received $293 in the forthcoming year, they will receive $343 in Child Tax Credits per child. This is nontaxable. Two-thirds of the Canadian women who receive the Family Allowance will benefit from this increased Child Tax Credit. This represents approximately two and a half million recipients.
Families with incomes, including combined family incomes where applicable, which are less than $26,330 in 1982 will receive the full Child Tax Credit. Families whose income is above that level will also qualify for the Child Tax Credit but only partially. The Child Tax Credit will vary on a decreasing scale, losing 5 per cent of income above that amount. The increase is being applied in such a way as to allow all those receiving the Child Tax Credit in any amount under the present system to receive an extra $50. For example, a mother with two children will receive an extra $100 up to a family income of approximately $38,000. This is how the present Child Tax Credit system functions. I will comment later on the ceiling at which the full Child Tax Credit is no longer applicable.
This additional $50 credit will commence at the beginning of the two-year special restraint period toward achieving a rate of inflation of only 6 per cent and 5 per cent. 1 have insisted that this credit be given immediately because it is important for mothers to know how their family budget will be affected.
The first Family Allowance cheque to come next year will be delivered at the end of the third week of January. While the amount for all those who receive Family Allowances will be more, the amount that one-third of those families who are more financially stable will receive will be more, but less than anticipated. That is why we have indicated that this legislation particularly affects mothers in high-income families.
For this reason I was surprised to hear the Fiouse Leader for the Official Opposition (Mr. Nielsen) announce a few minutes ago that his Party will vote against the Bill. 1 do not quite understand their reasoning for such a decision. I want my explanation to be clear in the event that some dimension of the Bill has escaped some Members of the House. Mothers will receive their Family Allowance cheques in a slightly lesser amount than would be the case with full indexing. At the beginning of January they can immediately apply for their Child Tax Credit. I point out that the mothers who can apply for Child Tax Credit immediately are those without income or with very low income. They do not really come under the income tax system. They are the ones most in need. These mothers will be the first to have their returns processed by Revenue Canada and will be the first to receive their Child Tax Credit in the mail. They will receive these Child Tax Credit cheues by March. The cheques which they will receive
December 1, 1982

in January and February will be more than, they are now, but slightly less than anticipated. The amount for January and February will be $28.52 for each child. However, two months later and continuing until the end of the usual income tax period they will receive a non-taxable Child Tax Credit which will be much larger than anticipated and far greater than last year's amount.
In other words, I think it is fair to say that, with the exception of the months of January and February when families will be missing $1.40 per child on each of their Family Allowance cheque, their Child Tax Credit cheques will be greater in the months of March, April or May.
There is another group that will not be affected by this Bill. They are the children who fall within the jurisdiction of welfare agencies, Government Departments or institutions. They are the children who fall under the category we call Special Allowances. These special allowances are paid on behalf of children under the age of 18 who are maintained by the agencies I have mentioned.
Since we have been very careful and have had the proper tools to protect not only the low income families but the middle income families as well, the savings from this restraint measure are relatively modest. They represent $70 million over two years. This could be explained by the fact that there will be a reduction in Family Allowances of $320 million over the two-year period; however, there will be an additional cost to make up for the loss which the Child Tax Credit will cost the Treasury, amounting to $250 million.
It seems to me that through this Bill we are clearly asking those families who can afford it to make some sacrifices, and not for the purpose of saving money. I want to insist that it has nothing to do with saving money, which was often stated as being the purpose of the Bill touching on the old age pension because of the Government deficit and all the rest. Rather, it is to bring about economic recovery and growth which will directly benefit all families far more by protecting them against the ravages, the erosion of their budgets simply as a result of high inflation. This is the purpose of the Bill.
1 have been here for days and have listened to horror stories which told of the results if Family Allowances were capped in the same way as were old age pensions for those who did not need the supplement. I think I will hear all sorts of arguments from Hon. Members opposite. They will make a long shopping list of everything that is wrong, to their way of thinking, in the child benefit system in Canada, or of any unmet need or problem that they recognize concerning families and children.

I know, because this is what happened during the debate on the bill to cap indexation of Old Age Security benefits of people who do not need the supplement. I am also aware that some Hon. Members will rise and have the nerve to say that by capping indexation of family allowances for families who are well off, and I am not referring to middle-income families but
Family Allowances Act, 1973
wealthy people, we are undermining the principle of universality. Hon. Members in both opposition parties said this when we were applying the same procedure to the pensions of individuals who do not need the supplement. It is quite clear, however, and I would like to remind-

-in particular, I would like to remind the leader of the New Democratic Party that, contrary to what he said publicly a few days ago, universality will not be affected at all by Bill C-132, which we are discussing right now. It will cap the indexation for families which are quite relatively well off. To say that Bill C-132 is part of an attempt to change the fundamental nature of family allowance is as ridiculous as saying that the six and five program, applied to increases in, say, the Bell telephone system, is an attempt to get rid of the telephone system. The logic is approximately as brilliant, as far as I can see.
Perhaps Hon. Members opposite think that when we applied the six and five program to ourselves, to our salaries as Members of Parliament, it was done to get rid of the Opposition. Maybe that was a wish expressed by some people in some quarters, but the logic is quite weak. I think everyone will see that it is not a very reasonable attempt to harm the Government, to pretend that the six and five program applied to the Family Allowances of those who do not need it in the first place, those who do not need the special help of the state, means a major change in the program.

I think people ought to know that Canada has one of the best child benefit systems in the world and that many countries in this present day and age would not be able to afford the benefits we have been providing for the children of Canada for years. For instance, France, which the Province of Quebec is always so eager to copy, France does not pay any family allowances to families with only one child, no matter what the circumstances are. In addition, the present Government in France is looking at new taxes as a way to cut its expenditures. Details are now being discussed, and there were reports last week in French weeklies including Le Point, L'Observateur, L'Express and in the newspaper Le Monde. France is now looking into a new tax measure under which families will be paying directly for their own family benefits, and this in addition to the present tax burden on all French families. I am not saying this to critize a foreign country, especially a country like France. In fact, I could say the same thing about West Germany, for instance, which also has family allowances. Just recently, I read that the West German Chancellor announced a proposal that will substantially reduce family allowances, and the worst part is that it will apply to families with more than two children. Belgium has just announced a temporary reduction in its family allowances, and there is a possibility that family allowances for the first child will be dropped. In other words, many countries are having to cope with the same economic difficulties as we are. I think it is very unfair, but I suppose it is to be expected in politics, that the Opposition is

December 1, 1982
Family Allowances Act, 1973
blasting the Government for poor management. Although there may be a difference in degree, the economic situation is pretty much the same in all western countries, and each country is making adjustments according to the ideology of the party in power.
We have decided that people who need help must get it. We have said time and time again that our first priority is to help those whose needs are greatest. 1 could add another word that could or should be the basis for any future changes in the family allowances program, and it is the word "redistribution". I think everybody knows what this means, but in any case, redistribution means taking from groups that have a lot and then making sure that they do not get anything until those who do not have anything at all have received a fair share. Perhaps 1 should be a little more specific with respect to family allowances.

When we speak of children and the federal Government, we speak of only one program, Family Allowances. In the recent past, but not for the first time, many rumours have fed a public debate which never took place except among the media or through editorials. However, the public debate which really never took place in our country was with regard to what is called being for or against universality of Family Allowances. I submit that this is not the proper terminology and is not the concept at stake at all. Universality is a problem in medicare. That is where it really applies. However, to my way of thinking as Minister of National Health and Welfare, what really applies, because of our social policies, is the objective of equity and redistribution and caring for those most in need. If we had the appropriate equipment in Parliament, I would be able to give Members a graphic, visual presentation of the three levels of child benefits that flow to families from the Government of Canada at the present time. We would see that the total sum of benefits received by families are not well distributed in terms of equity and redistribution.
Another question is, if it is not suitable, why do we not change it? That is another question which I will address shortly. There are three elements in the system. One is the well-known Family Allowance which is taxable and goes to every child in the country through his or her mother. Another is the Child Tax Credit, of which I must say we are very proud and which was introduced in 1978. It is a mechanism to distribute the benefits only to those with the least income. We could ask ourselves if it is "normal" that it is available up to such high income levels. I will ask that question in a few minutes. However, the concept is surely the best we could have worked out.
[ Translation]
When it was introduced, the child tax credit went to all families earning less than $18,000, and over and above that amount, the tax credit gradually dropped to zero. However, as a result of indexation, we have reached the point where the
child tax credit applies to children in families earning as much as $26,000 or more. That is a lot of money, and as a result, two-thirds of Canadian families are receiving the child tax credit. Low-income families receive the full family allowance, while in other cases, the allowance tends to be less, since it is taxable for other Canadian families. The child tax credit is received in addition to the family allowance. Both low- and middle-income families receive the full child tax credit, which gradually drops down to zero for families who do not need it at all. In addition to all this, and there is a problem here, we have what is called the personal deduction for dependent children, which is part of the income tax system. Either parent, depending on family circumstances, may claim the deduction. I do not remember the exact amount, but I think it is fairly high. I cannot find it in my notes, but I think it is substantial, and if I remember correctly, the exemption is at least $600 per child, or about that amount . . . $670 per child on the next tax return, I am told by my colleague from Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) and I thank her for this information. A tax exemption is the opposite of a tax credit. With a tax credit, the less you earn, the more you get, and with the tax exemption, the more you earn, the more you benefit, and this means that practically speaking, mothers with a family income of less than $10,000 never even see this money. The tax credit concept, a relatively modern one in the taxation system, was introduced about ten years ago and is gaining acceptance, although there is considerable resistance among fiscal experts. Thus, the child tax credit is extremely important because with it we have introduced an entirely new element in the fiscal system, a measure that is judged to be very significant in redistributing wealth and removing some of the social injustice in our society.
This is also the mechanism we will need one day to establish and deliver a guaranteed annual income. Speaking about the child tax credit, there are two matters about which I would like to say something. These changes may be an improvement, and this is what I want to ask. We also have to consider whether such a decision would be appropriate at this time when Canadians are very worried about the economy, when they need to tighten the family budget and to know where they are going. This is not an easy question to answer. The other change which I think might be an improvement has to do with the child tax credit and a double scale of benefits. The first thing we have to ask ourselves is whether or not it is right in our society that families with an income over $26,000 receive the full child tax credit. I do not ask this question because I think there is something wrong in making $26,000 or $27,000 a year. Quite the opposite, I am very happy for those who do and the more there are, the happier I will be, because it means that our society as a whole is richer. This has to be mentioned because it is important. I ask the question because of something I said in my speech on old age pensions and which, to my knowledge, was not picked up by any Member of the Opposition. Obviously, no federal or provincial Minister of Health and Welfare in this country or in other Western countries will
December 1, 1982

be able in the next few years to get more money from the Consolidated Revenue Fund, in other words, from the taxpayers' money to add to his or her programs. This is what I am trying to explain.
The hundreds of millions of dollars which I used to obtain for this purpose no longer exist. We shall have to rely increasingly on a method which I have used myself. I do not recall how the votes divided, but 1 presume-my colleagues will correct me if 1 am wrong-that it was with the agreement of whole House that the bill creating the child tax credit was passed late in the Fall of 1978. You may remember that everyone supported the bill, at least I think so. Everyone voted. 1 am not sure how the Progressive Conservatives voted, but I shall check on it and I hope for their sake that they had enough common sense to vote for it. I am sure that they would support it today, but 1 do not remember what they did at the time. 1 presume they supported the bill. With regard to the financing of the child tax credit Hon. Members will remember that I had to withdraw a special exemption of about $50 for each child and that I was also forced to limit family allowances that same year. We considered it better to make the redistribution within the child benefit structure than to delude ourselves that we could find hundreds of millions of dollars elsewhere. At the time, as Hon. Members will recall, I had to agree with the indexing of the ceiling for families eligible to the full child tax credit. The ceiling was $18,000.1 left it at $18,000 because each year it would allow a greater redistribution to poorer families. However, since politics is the art of the possible, this amount was indexed and it is now over $26,000, which means that two thirds of all Canadian mothers receive the child tax credit. I now ask this question and I ask it in earnest: Is this what we want? Because among those receiving the child tax credit many are over the poverty line. I have asked the other question to various groups who represent what we call small wage-earners and people on welfare.

As the Child Tax Credit is now such a large amount, mothers may tell us that it would be better for them to receive it more than once a year, possibly three or four times a year, or one day each month, because of the need in the family budget.
I resisted that, against much advice from professionals in the field when the Child Tax Credit was created because I thought, and mothers confirmed to me, that a large amount distributed once a year is precisely something for which low income families can never budget properly. It goes either for bicycles for the children, a washing machine or something else that is needed in the family.
Now that the amount is double what it was three years ago, it is worth asking the question. I asked the Anti-Poverty Organization to look into that problem and advise me accordingly.

I have repeatedly touched upon what I believe could be improvements in the child benefit system. I again stress there is no point in dreaming about hundreds of millions or billions of dollars, which only God knows where to find, to add to the budgets of these statutory programs. Instead, in the future we will have to look to improvements from within. The Family Allowance costs Canadians about $2.2 billion, of which close to half a billion dollars comes back through income taxes. The value of the Child Tax Credit is close to $1 billion in benefits. The Child Tax Exemption would be around $800 million.

Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I simply want to repeat that the universality or indexation of family allowances will not be affected. We are not doing away with indexation, we are keeping it for everybody. It is only being capped for all families that are relatively well-off, which means in fact only one third of all Canadian mothers. I should not have to apologize for this, because both the rich and the poor in our society are affected, the families in which a son, a brother, a husband or a wife may have lost his or her job due to the hard times, a main cause of which is the fact that the shopping dollar of every family is being eroded by inflation. What is better then for the people? To feed inflation and keep it at the 12 or 13 per cent level with full indexation or to take the bull by the horns and attack inflation head-on? Of course, it is to attack inflation, and anyone involved in public administration is aware of the need for psychological persuasion and a general mobilization, if inflation is to be wrestled to the ground. And this general mobilization, we in Canada have decided to achieve it through the six and five program. These figures, of course, have been chosen arbitrarily, but they should make it possible for us to cut the 12 and 10 per cent inflation rates by half and bring them down to 6 and 5 per cent. These are our objectives, and in order to achieve them, we are asking all those responsible for various areas in our society to follow suit.
That is why I am asking-and I make no excuse for it-all Hon. Members, including those in the Opposition, to join forces with us to vote in favour of Bill C-132, with the assurance that both Quebec and Alberta are prepared to amend their legislation accordingly, since Family Allowances Act of Alberta is different from ours. This type of co-operation between governments-I insist on this, because it is important-reflects a common effort to bring about an economic society in which inflation is under control.

Canadians from one end of the country to the other are making similar shopping lists. They are waiting for the opportunity to present them to the Government when it gets around to calling a general election. Then they will show this Government what it is doing wrong.
As the Minister said, this Bill is part of a package of three linked together which deal with limiting the indexing of Old Age Security, Family Allowances and superannuated public servants. It is one of three Bills which affects pensions and benefits to children. The Minister spoke about pensions and benefits to children, both in this House and in broadcasts outside this House.
When the first of these three measures was introduced-Bill C-131, which limited the indexing of old age pensions-in her remarks in the House the Minister told the senior citizens of this country that they should be the ones to lead the fight in the battle against inflation. That was her charge to the senior citizens of this country. In the course of that debate and in responding to the Minister, I made the point that what is needed is not a series of ad hoc Bills like this, but a comprehensive reform of our income security systems and our retirement income system. There should be a comprehensive analysis and reform of those systems so they meet the goals they were designed to meet, not only now but in the future.
It is clear to anyone who has looked at the income security system and the retirement income system that at the present time they are not meeting the goals for which they were designed. How can they when in this country over three million people are living below the poverty line? Those security systems are just not working. Much of the assistance is not being targeted to those most in need. In her remarks, the Minister made some reference to that. She said that through the security systems the income is not well distributed. I agree with her. Therefore, I urge her to get on with a comprehensive review of these programs.
But instead of reforming these systems, what does she do? Instead of reforming these systems so they better fulfil their purposes, the Government tries to impose a series of ad hoc measures which, unfortunately, will further distort and complicate those systems. What they will end up with as a result of these three Bills is that the anomalies and inequities presently in the system will be increased rather than diminished.
Having said that, I would like to proceed to the specifics of Bill C-132, an Act to amend the Family Allowances Act, yet another part of the so-called six and five restraint package which was announced in the budget last June. It sets monthly Family Allowance payments at 6 per cent above the 1982 level beginning January 1 of next year, and 5 per cent above the 1983 level, beginning January 1, 1984. Had the normal indexing procedure been followed, and assuming a 10 per cent
inflation rate in 1983, then Family Allowances would have been $1.48 per month more in 1983 and $3.05 per month more in 1984 that they would be if this Bill had not been introduced. What that amounts to, Mr. Speaker, is that over the two-year period this Bill will be in effect, mothers will lose $54 per child which they otherwise would have received.
Through this measure, as the Minister has said, the Government expects to save $320 million over the next two years. However, although it is not part of this Bill but was given extensive reference by the Minister in her comments, there is another measure which the former Minister of Finance introduced in his budget last June. That additional measure was that there would be a temporary increase of $50 per child in the refundable Child Tax Credit for the 1982 taxation year. On the one hand we have a program of deindexing Family Allowances, which is supposed to save the Government $320 million. Off-setting that is a temporary Child Tax Credit increase for next year which will cost the Government $250 million. The $50 increase, that one-shot temporary increase, will be available to mothers early in 1983.
These two measures, the deindexing of the Family Allowance which is incorporated in this Bill and the temporary increase in the Child Tax Credit, will mean that all families who qualify for the full Child Tax Credit-that is, those families with incomes below $26,300-will come out $32 per child ahead in 1983, and they will lose a little over $4 per child over the entire two-year period. Families who qualify for a partial Child Tax Credit will lose something between $4 and $54 per child over the two-year period. Those who do not qualify for any Tax Credit will lose the full $54. There will be, of course, a further loss when full indexing resumes in 1985: the base payment will have been permanently lowered.
I do not intend to speak at length on this Bill, but I would like to reiterate one point 1 made in speaking to the Bill on old age pension indexing just a few days ago, and that is that the Government's six and five restraint program is being applied in a most capricious and inequitable fashion. We have only to compare the treatment which the Government is meting out in the way it addresses the deindexing of old age pensions and the deindexing of Family Allowances to see this. The disparity between the sacrifice being asked of senior citizens and families with children betrays the callousness and lack of thought which went into these Bills.
1 spoke of this in the debate on the Bill on old age pensions, which took away the full indexing from the pensions of senior citizens, but it does bear repeating because the cold hard numbers which you associate with it clearly make this point. Assuming a continuing 10 per cent inflation, single old age pensioners with incomes of $9,000 will be asked to sacrifice $290 over the next two years. Not only that, they will continue to sacrifice in 1985 and after because the base for their future pensions will have been permanently lowered. The $290 which they are being asked to sacrifice represents, perhaps, a month's rent which they will have to find from some other source, if they can do so. That is what they are being asked to sacrifice.

What is the Minister asking a family with two children and an income of $26,000 to sacrifice? Under Bill C-132 which we are looking at today and its related budget measures, these families will be asked to sacrifice $8 during the same period. Moreover, the maximum sacrifice any family will be asked to make, no matter how high its income, will be $54 during the period that this Bill is in effect.
What a comparison of the impact of these Bills shows, Mr. Speaker, is that some families with children in Canada will be slightly better off in 1983, assuming the one-year increase in Child Tax Credit. Yet no senior citizen will be any better off than they are now, and this includes the 360,000 who have no income other than Old Age Security and the Guaranteed Income Supplement, because there are no off-setting measures for those at the lowest income levels as there are in the case of families with children. One is given a special benefit, the other is not. In addition, the 1.2 million senior citizens who do not receive the income supplement will be considerably worse off. That is the difference in the way this Government is approaching these two Bills. It simply will not accord the same treatment to the senior citizens of this country that it does to families with children.
1 ask the Minister, where is the equity there? How can the Minister justify this disparity? The answer, surely, Mr. Speaker, is that she cannot. In fact, she does not even try. What the Government does is ignore the difference in the way that it is imposing the six and five restraint program. It is pretending that no differences exist. And I may say the Government is becoming quite good at that because it has had lots of practice at that kind of hypocrisy.
The Government claimed earlier this year that it was not reducing its commitment to medicare and post-secondary education. At the same time, its own estimates showed that almost half a billion dollars less was being spent for these purposes, but it chooses to ignore that.
Take another case. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) claimed several times recently in this House that negotiations were proceeding with the Provinces on a new Canada health act.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on behalf of the New Democratic Party to oppose Bill C-132. This Bill, to amend the Family Allowances Program, is another imposition by the Government of six and five restraint. In Bill C-125 last spring, the Government attacked workers with the six and five restraint. Recently we debated Bill C-131, an attack on senior citizens with its restraint on the old age pension. Bill C-132 is an attack on Canada's children, our most important national resource. It is an attack on families who are suffering from the highest unemployment rate in our history. They need every cent of their monthly Family Allowance cheques to pay the extra cost of clothing and feeding their children.
The Bill is also a slap in the face for women. I am sorry that the Minister is not in the House at the moment to listen to this point. The Family Allowance cheque is sometimes the only cheque that many women in Canada receive in their own name. This has great significance, even for mothers in high income families.
Even more harmful from the point of view of this Party- and I did not hear the previous speaker refer to this matter-is the fact that this Bill, following upon Bill C-131 which capped indexing and eroded the universal old age pension, is a deliberate Liberal strategy to erode Canada's universal social security system, in this case Family Allowances.
The Minister denied this but then she quickly said that the purpose of the Bill was to gear the Family Allowance to lower income people. Of course, we are in favour of adequate support for low income people, but we are also in favour of a universal Family Allowance.
I strongly suspect the motives of the Government in this matter. The basic monthly Family Allowance has been a right in Canada since 1945 when, as a result of CCF pressure, it was first introduced in the House. It is not something that can be taken away at the whim of an uncaring Liberal Government or, for that matter, a Tory Government. The federal Government, by reducing the cost of living on Family Allowance
December 1, 1982

cheques, is signalling that it no longer gives priority to the maintenance of the Family Allowance Program to cover all families in Canada.
The Minister repeatedly denies this, but at the same time her application of this proposal enforces the point I just made. Last June 29, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) claimed that the June budget "fully protects the lowest income Canadians and the working poor". Only persons "who are not in need will be asked to share in the serious sacrifices which are required to bring our country out of the economic crisis". We agree with the National Council of Welfare which indicated that the social policy aspects of the June budget would adversely affect thousands of low income Canadians.
Family Allowances until now have been fully indexed, but the budget first, and now as expressed in Bill C-132, will limit indexation to 6 per cent in 1983 and to 5 per cent in 1984. If there had been no budget and no Bill C-132, Family Allowances would have been $358.44 per child in 1983. However, with the budget cutback it will now amount to only $342.24 per year. This reduction means a great deal to many families with children, including middle-income families. Let us not kid ourselves; it is not only low income families who are having trouble these days. Middle income families are suffering from the high cost of living, are being threatened with unemployment and are probably paying off mortgages at exorbitant interest rates. They are hit hard as well. If they have two or three children, of course it is difficult for them to manage.
The Minister stated that she chose to protect the Child Tax Credit which goes to low and middle income families by retaining full indexation to the cost of living. However, she failed to point out that the Child Tax Credit is an annual refund, whereas most families depend upon monthly Family Allowance cheques to cover the costs they face in purchasing clothes and school books and in putting food on the table for their children.
The $26.91 per child is little enough as a Family Allowance to help with the costs of raising children each month. It does not even pay for the cost of a pair of jeans which most children need today, or the expensive runners which they also require. Of course, the price of these items will increase far above 6 per cent during next year. I know many families who do not seem to be known by the Minister that urgently need their Family allowance cheques, not at the end of the month but before the end of the month, to put food on the table. I know many mothers who simply do not have food to feed their families. Their welfare cheques are gone on rent and other costs, and they desperately await their Family Allowance cheques to put food on the table. I am sure there are many people who are working part-time or on unemployment insurance who have the same problem. The Minister does not seem to realize how important this is.
Also I should like to say that even higher income families use the Allowance as an essential part of their monthly income, often as an allowance for teenagers or for educational expenses. With unemployment reaching the highest level in our history, there are many families who normally would not
Family Allowances Act, 1973
have relied on Family Allowance for basic survival but now really need it just to keep food on the table and clothe their children.
Children are a state responsibility; they are not only the responsibility of individual families. I refer back to the report of the National Agenda for Action in a book called "For Canada's Children", which was a result of a study by the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. It was put out by the Canadian Commission for the International Year of the Child. I see the Hon. Member for Laval (Mr. Roy) has left the House. He chaired that Standing Committee. He will recall that the Committee committed itself, and it thought the Government, to some major steps. This is what it said about children:
Children should be a first priority, but in the structure of the Government of Canada there is no place where they are a primary concern.
The Minister has given several examples of this recently. It continued:
Children are the responsibility of all levels of Government we elect to represent us. Children are not independent economic entities: they depend on the family for their economic welfare. The normal working of the economy and the economic policies of Government therefore tend to affect the child indirectly through the family.
Also it said:
Since the quality of life of Canadian families is inextricably linked with the economic decisions made by governments, a concerted effort should be made to ensure that the economic decision making process takes into account the wellbeing of the family and the child.
Unfortunately, the Government has ignored this sound advice from the Canadian Commission for the International Year of the Child. It has ignored it by not establishing a secretariat for children which the Commission recommended that could have certainly taken a stand on the matter before us today. Also the Government ignored the Commission Report in the development of its program of restraint and, in particular, in drafting the Bill before us.
The Family Allowance cheque traditionally recognizes the importance of children and families in Canada. It is the only means by which pay cheques and Unemployment Insurance cheques are topped up to allow for the cost of feeding and clothing children each month. Under our system a single person receives the same pay cheque as a married man or woman who has several mouths to feed. We have developed as a Canadian tradition, of which most of us are very proud, a way to adjust to additional size and responsibilities of families with the monthly Family Allowance cheque indexed to the increase in cost of living and with tax deductions for dependants.
Of course, the Family Allowance cheque is very important to all families, not only low income ones. Also I should like to say that the cheque is of particular significance to women, as I mentioned earlier. It is usually mothers who are the main parenting persons in the home. They are the persons who receive the Family Allowance cheque. For women who are full-time homemakers, often the Family Allowance cheque is the only one they receive in their own names. Perhaps many

speechtext:
The Family Allowance cheque is of particular significance to women. Increasingly in today's world homemakers and mothers who are in the home full-time or during a good part of their lives receive no recognition, and recognition today is usually in the form of remuneration, unlike it might have been in previous generations. About the only thing they get is a card on Mother's Day and the Family Allowance cheque. To reduce the cost of living by discontinuing the indexing of Family Allowance cheques is a slap in the face to the women of Canada and to full-time mothers. The Liberals in effect are telling mothers that they are not important. In other words, mothers are the ones who can be made to pay for inflation in Canada today. They are telling mothers that they can buy second-hand clothes for their kids at lower cost because they are not going to maintain indexing to keep up with the real cost of living. This is what the Liberals are saying to many mothers and families. It is a callous Liberal Government that says that. There are many other ways the Government could have saved money, and indeed brought money into the coffers, other than by taking this means in a period of recession.
In the future, if our economy improves-if it ever does-I would like to see us consider the possibility of increasing the Family Allowance to an amount which more adequately would recognize the parenting role of a mother or a father in the home. An increased allowance, when we can afford this, could help cover the cost of daycare for a working parent or could be a means for full-time homemakers to pay into the Canada Pension Plan in their own names. We will be debating this point when we get around to the Green Paper on pension reform.
Recently I attended hearings of the New Democratic Party Task Force on Older Women. These hearings were held in every province of Canada. A woman in Fredericton proposed that the monthly Family Allowance should be raised to a minimum of $200 per family per month so that women could have the choice to remain in the home to care for family members full time and have some financial recognition, not a full wage, but some recognition for this labour. It could also
provide the means for some homemakers to pay into the Canada Pension Plan on their own behalf. For mothers who work it could help to pay for daycare costs. If we believe that children are our greatest resource and that parents should have a choice of how they care for their children, this is indeed a very interesting proposal. One caution in that regard is that we do not want changes which would increase the ghettoizing of women in the home and would further exploit their labour as has traditionally been done in the case of homemakers.
We in this Party believe that we must retain the full Family Allowance, paid monthly, and that a monthly payment is essential for each child. It should increase as soon as the economy can allow for this. In order to finance this universal allowance more equitably, we have a proposal which I did not hear the Minister mention at all, nor did I hear the Hon. Member from the Conservative Party mention it. We propose that the financing of this universal program-and the same thing applies to old age pensions-could be paid for more equitably through a reform in the tax system. The highest income people in society would repay the full amount through a more realistic income tax system. We are opposed absolutely to a means test for Family Allowances for the same reason that we oppose a means test for old age pensions. A means test stigmatizes people. It adds to bureaucratic costs. It is far better to reform the tax system and tax back the allowances from wealthier families while maintaining a universal Family Allowance Program as a right.
Both the old age pension cheques and Family Allowance cheques are not socked away in the bank. The money received from them goes immediately into consumer goods and is recycled within our economy. Indeed, this is a stimulus to small business and certainly helps to maintain jobs. Those allowances are important from an economic point of view as well as a social right.
The NDP stands solidly behind universal social security for Canadians. We fought for adequate pensions, pensions above the poverty line, and we will continue to do so by resisting the imposition of six and five on the basis of the old age pension.
We fought for the right of workers to unemployment insurance and disability coverage. We are proud that we have a Program now. Compare the tragedy we would be in if we were back in the same situation as workers were in the 1930s.
Universal medicare was pioneered by Tommy Douglas in Saskatchewan. Medicare is now available to all Canadians. Finally, in 1945 after considerable pressure from the CCF and the labour movement, universal Family Allowances were initiated. These allowances became taxable in 1973, but their being taxable meant that only a portion of the allowance is returned through our income tax system.
We know that the wealthiest people in society pay no income tax at all. That is where the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) can get more money for her restraint program instead of taking the money from the backs of children and families.
December !, 1982

1 repeat, Family Allowances are a right. Family Allowances must not be considered welfare. They must be fully indexed to the real cost of living, not to a six and five reduction in the cost of living beginning next year. Since the Liberals want to target those most in need, why do the Liberals not reform the tax system and have the higher income people pay more and the lower income people receive more? Of course, we are in favour of the Child Tax Credit system. In fact, we would like to see this system expanded to a guaranteed annual income. That is not to say that we should not have a universal Family Allowance Program as we have described it.
The Liberals, through Bill C-132, are signalling to us and to Canadians their willingness to erode the universal Family Allowance system in Canada. The Minister can deny this, but we have quotes from the former Minister of National Health and Welfare who is now the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). On November 3, 1982, he said:
The Government may end universality of the family allowance program but will not cut old age security benefits.
According to the article, we find:
Lalonde said in an interview he disagrees with some of his colleagues who say universal social programs are a basic principle of Liberal philosophy.
And he believes Canadians may be ready to swallow an end to universality of family allowance in which all parents, regardless of income, receive monthly benefits. He thinks they may be ready to accept that such benefits should go to those most in need.
Another sentence from this article reads:
But he said family allowance is an open issue on which he hopes there will be a cool-headed, rational debate.
When our leader questioned him in the House a few days later, the Minister began to back down and waffle and said that he was not abandoning the principle of universality but he still was going to keep an open mind on this question.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare can say all she likes about retaining universality, but that does not sound like a very permanent commitment to us.
We also know from press reports that the Liberal Government during the summer, and the Cabinet in particular, was considering the whole concept of universality as it affected old age pensions as well. The Liberals, being very pragmatic, did not have the guts to go against the political reality, and when they heard from their supporters, even Liberal Members from right across the country as well as middle-income and higher income people, that they would not tolerate a cut in the Family Allowances, this is when the Liberals backed down. It is not because they believe in the Family Allowance in principle. No, that has never come into the question at all. It is simply political pragmatism, as it is with the Conservatives.
Speaking of Conservatives, 1 would like to know what their position is on universal social programs. The Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) said not a word about this. All she talked about was the ad hocery of programs and the specific amount. She did not once affirm that the Conservative Party believes in universal Family Allowances for Canadians. Indeed, we have information which indicates that when the Tories were in Government very briefly in 1969, they
Family Allowances Act, 1973
had already begun a process to dismantle the universal Family Allowance Program.
